rows.speaker: بعض نسائه
rows.claim: A wife unable to visit the Prophet was told to send lamp oil for the mosque; doing so earned the reward of praying there.
rows.anchor: عن بعض نسائه عليه الصلاة والسلام أنها قالت

rows.speaker: رسول الله ﷺ
rows.claim: The Prophet identifies the Sacred Mosque as first and al-Aqsa as second, established forty years later.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله أي مسجد وضع في الأرض أولا قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob founded al-Aqsa after Abraham built the Kaaba; Solomon later renewed it or completed his father's renewal.
rows.anchor: وقد أسسه يعقوب عليه السلام بعد بناء إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Isra raised Muhammad to heaven to witness great wonders; he ascended from Jerusalem's rock, met prophets in each heaven, and saw Paradise, Hell, and innumerable angels.
rows.anchor: أي لنرفعه إلى السماء حتى يرى ما يرى من العجائب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports Muhammad saw an unending armed host on dappled horses, each man and horse a thousand years long; Gabriel identified them as God's hosts, known only to God.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad led the prophets in prayer at Jerusalem; al-ʿAqāʾiq says two rakʿahs, while another view calls it supplication and describes seven rows, including three messengers, with angels joining.
rows.anchor: وقد صلى صلى الله عليه وسلم بالأنبياء عليهم السلام في بيت المقدس قال في العقائق

rows.speaker: القاضي زكريا
rows.claim: Al-Qadi Zakariyya says this unique prayer displayed Muhammad as imam of all prophets.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي زكريا في شرح الروض والحكمة في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars differed whether Muhammad led prophets' spirits alone or their bodies too, and whether before or after ascent; Ibn Kathir preferred after, Qadi Iyad and others before.
rows.anchor: وهل صلى بأرواحهم خاصة أو بها خاصة أو بها مع الأجساد فيه خلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Muhammad prayed two rakʿahs in every heaven, leading its angels.
rows.anchor: وجاء في رواية أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام صلى في كل سماء ركعتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Isra and ascent occurred in one portion of one night; Muhammad returned by the same route, and the duration is unspecified.
rows.anchor: وكان الإسراء والعروج في بعض ليلة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports say Muhammad found his bed still warm when he returned.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم لما رجع وجد فراشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says a branch struck by Muhammad's turban on departure was still moving when he returned.
rows.anchor: إن غصن شجرة أصابه بعمامته في ذهابه فلما رجع وجده بعد يتحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though some separate the Isra and Miʿraj into different nights, the verse's apparent sense places them in one night, with Jerusalem preceding the ascent.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن ليلة الإسراء غير ليلة المعراج وظاهر الآية على ما سمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for first going to Jerusalem is that the Prophet reached sacred places gradually, since Jerusalem was less exalted than the heavenly presence.
rows.anchor: ليكون وصوله إلى الأماكن الشريفة على التدريج فإن شرف بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the Isra prepared Muhammad for the extraordinary ascent, although the Isra itself was wondrous.
rows.anchor: توطينا له عليه الصلاة والسلام لما في المعراج من الغرابة العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says the route honored the land of resurrection through the Prophet's departure and return.
rows.anchor: لتتشرف به أرض المحشر ذهابا وإيابا

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār reports an open gate from the lowest heaven to Jerusalem through which seventy thousand angels descend daily to seek forgiveness for its visitors; the Isra made the ascent straight upward.
rows.anchor: فقد نقل عن كعب الأحبار أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says the mosque's pillars longed to meet Muhammad, so his journey began there to answer their wish promptly.
rows.anchor: اسطوانات المسجد قالت ربنا حصل لنا من كل نبي حظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says Jerusalem's heavenly gate lies opposite the rock, so the Prophet's ascent was straight.
rows.anchor: ثم عرج به ليكون صعوده على الاستواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partitive min signals that God showed Muhammad only some signs because His signs are limitless; saying signs without min might suggest all of them.
rows.anchor: وعبر بمن الدالة على التبعيض لأن أراءة جميع آيات الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection compares Muhammad's partial vision with Abraham's vision of the heavenly dominion; one answer is that some divine signs surpass that dominion, as 53:18 says.
rows.anchor: واستشكل بأنه كيف يرى نبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم بعض الآيات

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji says the objection fails: Abraham saw proofs within the cosmos, which do not rival the Miʿraj.
rows.anchor: السؤال غير وارد لأن ما رآه إبراهيم عليه السلام ما فيها من الدلائل والحجج

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya suggests the verse may mean Muhammad himself was shown to people as one of God's signs; al-Alusi calls this extremely remote.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون معنى الآية لنري محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم للناس آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not indicate that Muhammad saw God on the Isra, since God is not one of His signs; supporters rely on other evidence.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس في الآية إشارة إلى أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم رأى ربه ليلة الإسراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse explicitly states the Isra, not Miʿraj, since its signs can refer only to events on the journey to Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وكذا ليست الآية لصافي المعراج بل هي نص في الإسراء دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say no verse explicitly establishes the Miʿraj: denying the Qurʾān-confirmed Isra is disbelief, whereas denying Miʿraj makes one an innovator, not an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: ليس في الآيات مطلقا ما هو نص في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Khazin says the Qurʾān mentioned Jerusalem alone to avoid provoking denial of the ascent; after people confirmed Jerusalem's signs, the Isra served as a prelude to reporting Miʿraj.
rows.anchor: أن فائدة ذكر المسجد الأقصى فقط دون السماء أنه لو ذكر صعوده عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the later indication suffices as explicit mention.
rows.anchor: إن الإشارة بعد ذلك للتصريح كافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from third-person asrā bi-ʿabdihi to majestic first-person baraknā and nuriyahu magnifies the blessings and signs.
rows.anchor: وصرف الكلام من الغيبة التي في قوله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third person suits passage from the visible world to the unseen; first-person plural magnifies God's blessing, and the wording's movement marks arrival and return to the unseen.
rows.anchor: يدل على مسيره عليه الصلاة والسلام من عالم الشهادة إلى عالم الغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final pronoun in inna-hu most likely refers to God, matching abdihi; God knows the servant's words and sees purified, sincere deeds worthy of nearness.
rows.anchor: على تقدير كون الضمير له تعالى كما هو الأظهر وعليه الأكثر

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi says God hears the servant's speech and sees deeds purified of desire, truthful and sincere, worthy of nearness.
rows.anchor: أنه هو السميع لأقوال ذلك العبد البصير بأفعاله

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: A minority reading takes the pronoun to refer to Muhammad, who hears God's speech and sees God, or sees creation and the signs shown to him, as in 53:17.
rows.anchor: كما نقله أبو البقاء عن بعضهم

rows.speaker: الجلبي
rows.claim: Al-Jalabi says Muhammad as the referent is not impossible; this makes him hear divine commands and observe creation or displayed signs.
rows.anchor: إنه لا يبعد والمعنى عليه إن عبدي الذي شرفته

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi suggests the possible double reference hints that Muhammad saw and heard the Lord through God, as in the cited report.
rows.anchor: ولعل السر في مجيء الضمير محتملا للأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic huwa may distinguish God's hearing without an ear and sight without an eye, or signal Muhammad's special honor.
rows.anchor: وتوسيط ضمير الفصل إما لأن سماعه تعالى بلا أذن

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reads the closing phrase as a warning to disbelievers: God hears their denial of the Isra and sees their deeds, so He will punish them.
rows.anchor: وعيد للكفار على تكذيبهم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في أمر الإسراء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads liyuriyahu with third-person yāʾ, producing four shifts of person in the verse.
rows.anchor: بياء الغيبة ففي الآية حينئذ أربع التفاتات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book given to Moses is the Torah; making it guidance means either the Book itself, the apparent reading, or Moses.
rows.anchor: الكتاب وهو الظاهر أو موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause to Israelites attaches to guidance or making it guidance; the wāw resumes the sentence or coordinates with the opening glorification, not with asrā.
rows.anchor: متعلق بهدى أو بجعل واللام تعليلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses verse is an excursus preparing for the Qurʾān: Moses received the Torah on his journey to the mount, was spoken to and honored as interlocutor, paralleling Muhammad's journey while underscoring the difference between their books and recipients.
rows.anchor: وعقب آية الإسراء بهذه استطرادا تمهيدا لذكر القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command may explain what the Book contains: do not take another protector besides God; another analysis supplies an omitted command phrase.
rows.anchor: على أن أن تفسيرية ولا ناهية والتفسير كما قال أبو البقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bahr allows infinitive an with an omitted preposition, yielding so that they would not take; another view makes the clause a substitute for al-kitāb.
rows.anchor: وجوز في البحر أن تكون أن مصدرية والجار قبلها محذوف

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa allows an to be extra and makes the prohibition depend on omitted speech; Abu Hayyan rejects it because this is not a place for extra an.
rows.anchor: أبو البقاء أن تكون زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that lā is extra, as in 7:12, is unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وكذا جوز أن تكون ( لا ) زائدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، عيسى، أبو رجاء، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers recite an lā yattakhidhūna with third-person yāʾ; Shaykhzada finds neither an explanatory parsing with yāʾ nor an infinitival parsing with direct address satisfactory.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس ومجاهد وعيسى وأبو رجاء وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wakīl is a lord entrusted with one's affairs; God is called Wakil for sufficing for and caring for servants, not as a subordinate to a superior client.
rows.anchor: أي ربا تكلون إليه أموركم غيري فالوكيل فعيل بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is taken as an extra emphatic preposition and dun means other than; a partitive reading is allowed but the first is preferred, prohibiting association with God.
rows.anchor: استظهر الأول والمراد النهي عن الإشراك به تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhurriyyata is accusative by specification or vocative; the address recalls God saving their ancestors in Noah's Ark when they had no protector but Him.
rows.anchor: نصب على الاختصاص أو على النداء والمراد الحمل على التوحيد

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki says the vocative analysis fits direct address but awkwardly clashes with third-person yattakhidhūna; al-Alusi says the attempted rebuttal does not remove the difficulty.
rows.anchor: وخص مكي النداء بقراءة الخطاب قال : من قرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhurriyyata may instead be one object of take, with wakīlan as the other; it may substitute for wakīlan, prohibiting worship of figures such as Ezra and Jesus.
rows.anchor: لأن المبدل منه ليس في حكم الطرح من كل الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them Noah's descendants recalls the ancestors' rescue, their weakness and need to be carried, and the descendants' greater weakness.
rows.anchor: وفي التعبير بما ذكر إيماء إلى علة النهي من أوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa calls dhurriyyata a substitute for Musa, but al-Alusi regards that construction as very remote.
rows.anchor: أبو البقاء كونه بدلا من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading may be predicate of an omitted subject or substitute for the pronoun in yattakhidhūna; Ibn Atiyya objects for direct address, while Abu Hayyan details allowed constructions.
rows.anchor: على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هو ذرية

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت، أبان بن عثمان، زيد بن علي، مجاهد
rows.claim: They transmit kasra on the dhāl; Mujahid also transmits fatḥa, and Zayd has a form with fatḥa, light rāʾ, and doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن ثابت وأبان بن عثمان وزيد بن علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In inna-hu the pronoun most naturally refers to Noah, abundantly grateful in all circumstances.
rows.anchor: كثير الشكر في مجامع حالاته

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: Salman says Noah thanked God whenever he put on clothes or ate; al-Hakim authenticated this report.
rows.anchor: سلمان الفارسي قال : كان نوح عليه السلام إذا لبس ثوبا

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrahim says Noah's gratitude was to say God's name before eating and praise Him afterward.
rows.anchor: إبراهيم قال : شكره عليه السلام أن يسمي إذا أكل

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: A report from Muadh ibn Anas says Noah was called grateful because he recited the praise in 30:17–18 morning and evening.
rows.anchor: معاذ بن أنس الجهني عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : إنما سمى

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: A report from Aisha says Noah never rose from relieving himself without thanking God for pleasure, retained benefit, and removed harm; al-Alusi calls it part of Noah's gratitude.
rows.anchor: عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : إن نوحا لم يقم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of Noah's gratitude hints that God rescued his companions through its blessing and urges descendants to imitate him and shun shirk, the greatest unbelief.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الجملة إيماء بأن إنجاء من معه عليه السلام كان ببركة شكره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows the Noah clause to be an aside; its link would then be only that Noah was already mentioned.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري : يجوز أن يقال ذلك عند ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun in inna-hu to refer to Moses, as a reason for the Book, guidance, or prohibition; al-Alusi finds this remote.
rows.anchor: عائد على موسى عليه السلام والجملة مسوقة على وجه التعليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains wa-qadaynā ilā as We informed Israel; al-Raghib adds decisive revelation, and grammarians say the verb includes revelation.
rows.anchor: أخرج بن جرير وغيره عن ابن عباس أي أعلمناهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas takes ilā as ʿalā, so the decree was imposed upon them.
rows.anchor: إلى بمعنى على وروى ذلك أيضا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-kitāb most naturally means the Torah; the plural reading al-kutub allows a generic Book or the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: أو الجنس بدليل قراءة أبي العالية وابن جبير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: As related by Tawus, Ibn Abbas invoked this verse against deniers of divine decree, threatening to seize any Qadari present and recite it.
rows.anchor: طاوس قال : كنت عند ابن عباس ومعنا رجل من القدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corruption clause answers an unspoken oath and omits the decree's object: God decreed their corruption and arrogance; alternatively, the decree itself is construed like an oath.
rows.anchor: جواب قسم محذوف وحذف متعلق القضاء أيضا للعلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-arḍ may mean the earth generally or the land of Syria and Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالأرض الجنس أو أرض الشام وبيت المقدس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، نصر بن علي، جابر بن زيد
rows.claim: Their passive reading means Israel would be corrupted by others through misguidance or domination.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس ونصر بن علي وجابر بن زيد

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: Isa's active reading means Israelites themselves would corrupt the land through sins.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى ( لتفسدن ) بفتح التاء وضم السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marratayn is an accusative verbal noun referring to two acts of corruption.
rows.anchor: مرتين ( منصوب على أنه مصدر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi, transmitting from his teachers, identifies the first corruption as Zechariah's killing; after he warned them, a story says they found and sawed through the tree where he hid.
rows.anchor: أولاهما على ما نقل السدي عن أشياخه قتل زكريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Israelites killed Zechariah because they suspected him over Mary's pregnancy.
rows.anchor: سبب قتله أنهم اتهموه بمريم عليها السلام

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq identifies Isaiah as the first victim, killed after fleeing into a tree; he says Zechariah died naturally.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحق هي قتل شعيا عليه السلام وقد بعث بعد موسى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari identifies the first corruption as killing Zechariah and imprisoning Jeremiah, the second as killing John and attempting to kill Jesus; al-Alusi objects Jeremiah lived over two centuries earlier.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أولاهما قتل زكريا وحبس أرميا والآخرة قتل يحيى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A preferred account makes first corruption alteration and neglect of Torah, with Jeremiah imprisoned and wounded for warning them and prophesying Muhammad; the second is killing Zechariah and John.
rows.anchor: إنه الحق أن الأولى تغيير التوراة وعدم العمل بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who say Zechariah died naturally identify only John as victim in the second corruption.
rows.anchor: إن زكريا مات في فراشه اقتصر على يحيى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: One report says a king sought an unlawful marriage; after John forbade it, the woman's mother told her to demand John's blood, and the king beheaded him; his blood boiled until seventy thousand were killed.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس وغيره أن سبب ذلك أن ملكا أراد أن يتزوج

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas says the king's wife tried to seduce handsome John; after he refused, she told her daughter to ask for his head, and the king granted it.
rows.anchor: الربيع بن أنس : إن يحيى عليه السلام كان حسنا جميلا

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i says God did not identify the two corruptions, so no reported identification can be asserted with certainty.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى ذكر فسادهم في الأرض مرتين ولم يبين ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their great arrogance means pride against obeying God or oppressive domination; the root means elevation, figuratively tyranny.
rows.anchor: لتستكبرن عن طاعة الله تعالى أو لتغلبن الناس بالظلم والعدوان

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads ʿaliyyan with kasra and doubled yāʾ; al-Bahr says sound verbal nouns more often preserve this form than plurals.
rows.anchor: زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first promise is when punishment for the first corruption arrived; waʿd can mean promised punishment, threat, or appointed time.
rows.anchor: والوعد بمعنى الموعود مراد به العقاب كما في البحر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God let the attackers act without restraining them; al-Alusi sees an implicit Muʿtazilite agenda.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري : خلينا بينهم وبين ما فعلوا ولم نمنعهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says God may have sent an emissary to the attackers' king ordering invasion, making their attack divinely commissioned.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية : يحتمل أن يكون الله تعالى أرسل إلى ملك أولئك العباد

rows.speaker: الحسن، زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read ʿabīdan, a variant form for God's servants.
rows.anchor: الحسن وزيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attackers had exceptional strength in battle; al-Raghib distinguishes baʾs as combat violence and calls severe force emphatic or intensive.
rows.anchor: ذوي قوة وبطش في الحروب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، قتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada identify attackers as Jalut al-Jazari and troops.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس وقتادة هم جالوت الجزري وجنوده

rows.speaker: ابن جبير، ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn Ishaq identify them as Sennacherib, king of Babylon, and his army.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير وابن إسحاق هم سنجاريب ملك بابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other identities are the Amalekites or Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon's governor for Loharasp, sent after Israel rejected and wounded Jeremiah; one account calls this correct.
rows.anchor: وفي الأعلام للسهيلي هم بختنصر عامل لهراسف أحد ملوك الفرس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jasū khilāl al-diyār means moving through houses to search for Israelites; al-Raghib compares it to ḥāsū and dāsū.
rows.anchor: أي ترددوا وسطها لطلبكم

rows.speaker: أبو السمال، طلحة
rows.claim: Abu al-Sammal and Talha read ḥāsū with ḥāʾ; another reading has tajassasū with jīm.
rows.anchor: بالحاء أبو السمال وطلحة وقريء أيضا

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd defines jās and ḥās as seeking exhaustively; khilāl may be singular or a plural of khalal.
rows.anchor: أبو زيد : الجوس والحوس طلب الشيء باستقصاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most accounts say attackers destroyed the Temple, massacred, exiled, captured Israelites, and burned the Torah; Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say they entered and withdrew without fighting.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن في هذه البعثة خرب هؤلاء العباد بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-karrata means restored power and victory, figuratively derived from returning; alayhim attaches to victory or may attach to the verb.
rows.anchor: الدولة والغلبة وأصل معنى الكر العطف والرجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past tense expresses certainty; some say a hundred years passed before Israel regained power after repentance.
rows.anchor: وهذا على ما في البحر إخبار منه تعالى في التوراة لبني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says Bahman son of Isfandiyar restored captives brought to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, returned them to Syria, and appointed Daniel over them.
rows.anchor: فرد أسراءهم الذين أتى بهم بختنصر إلى بابل وسيرهم إلى أرض الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says a Babylon conqueror, moved by his Israelite wife, returned surviving Israelites to their homeland; later prophets helped restore them.
rows.anchor: في البحر أن ملكا غزا أهل بابل وكان بختنصر قد قتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies restored victory with David's defeat of Goliath; al-Alusi objects that David built the Temple only afterward.
rows.anchor: رد الكرة بأن سلط الله تعالى داود عليه السلام فقتل جالوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply that mosque means sacred ground or uses semantic substitution is strained; al-Alusi says the Temple existed before David.
rows.anchor: ودفع بأن حقيقة المسجد الأرض لا البناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God replenished their plundered wealth and returned their captured children, making them more numerous than before or their enemies.
rows.anchor: كثيرة بعد ما نهبت أموالكم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim takes nafir as the household and kin who go out with a man.
rows.anchor: والنفير على ما قال أبو مسلم كالنافر من ينفر مع الرجل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows nafir to be a collective plural for a group assembling to go to battle.
rows.anchor: الزجاج : يجوز أن يكون جمع نفر ككلب وكليب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others parse nafir as the verbal noun for going to battle and cite poetry; al-Suhayli prefers collective noun usage.
rows.anchor: هو مصدر أي أكثر خروجا إلى الغزو كما في قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doing good for oneself or others benefits the doer through reward; wrongdoing returns on the doer through punishment.
rows.anchor: أعمالكم سواء كانت لازمة لأنفسكم أو متعدية للغير أي علمتموها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read lām in falahā as ʿalā; al-Tabari says it means ilā, returning wrongdoing to the self.
rows.anchor: الطبري : هي بمعنى إلى على معنى فإساءتها راجعة إليها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the lām as restriction; al-Alusi says this need not deny worldly harms to others, since afterlife reward and punishment do not transfer.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أنها للاختصاص وتعقب بأنه مخالف لما في الآثار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings make the lām entailment, as in 3:91, or ironically a benefit even in wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: إنها للاستحقاق كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broader reading includes deeds for oneself or others; iḥsān means doing what is fitting and good for self and others, wrongdoing the opposite.
rows.anchor: وتعميم الإحسان ومقابله بحيث يشملان المتعدي واللازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating iḥsān but not wrongdoing hints that good is more prevalent and deserves repetition.
rows.anchor: تكرير الإحسان في النظم الكريم دون الإساءة إشارة إلى أن جانب الإحسان أغلب

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali said he had neither done good nor evil to anyone, then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه قال : ما أحسنت إلى أحد

rows.speaker: القطب
rows.claim: Al-Qutb connects the verse to Israel's history: disobedience brought plunder and captivity, while repentance and obedience improved their condition.
rows.anchor: على ما قال القطب أنه لما عصوا سلط الله تعالى عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the second punishment arrived, attackers made Israel's faces show grief; face may mean the literal face, whole person, or leaders, though al-Alusi favors literal faces.
rows.anchor: أي ليجعل العباد المبعوثون آثار المساءة والكآبة بادية في وجوهكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording li-yasūʾū is chosen over the shorter form to combine bodily suffering with psychological distress, reinforced by the destruction clause.
rows.anchor: واختير هذا على ليسوؤكم مع أنه أخصر وأظهر إشارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second idhā signals punishment came after Israel's numbers and resources grew, displaying ingratitude before God surprised them; it warns against sudden punishment.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على أن مجيء وعد عقاب المرة الآخرة لم يتراخ عن كثرتهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر، ابن عامر، حمزة
rows.claim: They read li-yasūʾa in the singular; its subject can be God, the promise, or implied sending, with only God literal.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر وابن عامر وحمزة

rows.speaker: علي، زيد بن علي، الكسائي
rows.claim: Their reading li-nasūʾa with majestic first-person nūn makes God the only possible referent.
rows.anchor: قراءة علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وزيد بن علي والكسائي

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads li-nasūʾanna with imperative lām and light emphatic nūn; an imperative clause with elided fāʾ answers idhā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي ( لنسوءن ) بلام الأمر ونون العظمة

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali also transmits emphatic nūn/yāʾ readings, where the lām is an oath and its clause stands for the conditional response.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أيضا ( لنسوءن وليسوءن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in waliyadkhulu is purposive and attaches to omitted baʿathnā; other syntax attaches it elsewhere, and on command or oath readings it can serve those functions.
rows.anchor: لام كي والجار والمجرور معطوف على الجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-masjid means Jerusalem's Temple; Arabic can treat a destination as direct object after dropping ilā, as in dakhaltu al-bayt.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح أن الصحيح في نحو دخلت البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entry like the first time means with swords, force, victory, and humiliation; this challenges accounts that the first invasion involved no fighting or looting.
rows.anchor: التشبيه على ما في البحر أنهم يدخلونه بالسيف والقهر والغلبة والإذلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yutabbirū means utterly destroy; Qutrub glosses it as demolish, and poetry supports undoing what was built.
rows.anchor: أي يهلكوا وقال قطرب : يهدموا وأنشد قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says tatbīr is a Nabataean word.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير أن التتبير كله نبطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā ʿalaw refers to what attackers conquered; alternatively it is temporal, meaning as long as they remained dominant, and tatbīran means utter destruction.
rows.anchor: الذي غلبوه واستولوا عليه فما اسم موصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many identify the second attackers as Nebuchadnezzar and his army, but al-Suhayli objects John died after Jesus' ascension, long after Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: غير واحد : إنهم بختنصر وجنوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alexander and his army are another proposal, rejected because he lived about three centuries before Jesus; Nebuchadnezzar remains possible if the first corruption killed Isaiah.
rows.anchor: وقيل الاسكندر وجنوده وتعقبه أيضا بأن بين الاسكندر وعيسى

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr reports King Khardush attacked them, with his commander responsible for killing them over John's blood.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن الزبير رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن الذي غزاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says the commander found blood boiling in the sanctuary; Israelites revealed it was John's blood, and it stopped after he asked John to quiet it before everyone was killed.
rows.anchor: صاحب الجيش دخل مذبح قرابينهم فوجد فيه دما يغلي

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf prefers Bayardus, a late Successor King, and suggests he is the Khardush mentioned above.
rows.anchor: إن المبعوث عليهم في المرة الثانية بيردوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Successor Kings arose after Alexander defeated Darius; over seventy ruled for 512 years before Persia reunited under Ardashir son of Babak, placing John's killer among their later rulers.
rows.anchor: وهؤلاء الملوك ظهروا بعد قتل الإسكندر دارا واستيلائه على ملك الفرس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Chronologies place Alexander's victory 435 years after Nebuchadnezzar and Jesus' birth about 300 years after Alexander; John's killing and second attack came later, over 735 years after the first.
rows.anchor: ففي بعض التواريخ أن قتل الإسكندر دارا بعد بختنصر بأربعمائة

rows.speaker: اليهود
rows.claim: The Jewish account dates the first attack to Jeremiah's time: Israel imprisoned and wounded him, Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the Temple in his nineteenth year, it remained ruined seventy years before Titus destroyed it; they put 490 years between attacks.
rows.anchor: والذي ذهب إليه اليهود أن المبعوث أولا بختنصر وكان في زمن آرميا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exact identities and dates are not central; the lesson is that repeated disobedience leads God to send avengers.
rows.anchor: إن معرفة الأقوام المبعوثين بأعيانهم وتاريخ البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's surface sense suggests the same servants made both attacks; those who distinguish them compare pronoun return to saying I have a dirham and its half.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يقتضي اتحاد المبعوثين أولا وثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may show mercy after the second attack if Israel repents; if they return to corruption, He punishes them as before, and the conditional warns them not to return.
rows.anchor: إن تبتم وانزجرتم عن المعاصي

rows.speaker: الحسن، قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada say Israel returned to sin by rejecting the Prophet and plotting to kill him, so God punished Qurayza, expelled Nadir, and imposed tribute on the rest.
rows.anchor: وقد عادوا بتكذيب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقصدهم قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Persian kings later punished Israel by imposing tribute and other burdens.
rows.anchor: وقيل عادوا فعاد الله تعالى بأن سلط عليهم الأكاسرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others gloss ḥaṣīran as prison; a line by Labid is cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس وغيره : أي سجنا وأنشد في البحر قول لبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaṣīr may mean an enclosure surrounding them, though its active form would ordinarily match gender; explanations include relational feminine, passive sense, or construing Hell as masculine.
rows.anchor: وإن كان بمعنى حاصر أي محيط بهم وفعيل بمعنى فاعل

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib links ḥaṣīr to woven matting whose strips constrain one another, so it can mean confined; he also records the sense ruler.
rows.anchor: الراغب : كأنه جعل الحصير المرمول وأطلق عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading ḥaṣīr as a ruler who blocks access is too remote for the verse, despite its possible subtle meaning.
rows.anchor: وحمل ما في الآية على ذلك مما لم تعرض له والحمل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording says Hell is for unbelievers, rather than for you, marking Israel's return as unbelief and the cause of judgment.
rows.anchor: وكان الظاهر أن يقال لكم بدل للكافرين إلا أنه عدل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also interprets ḥaṣīr as bed or resting place; the word may denote tightly woven matting, and its rhetoric is a concise comparison.
rows.anchor: فسر ذلك بالفراش والمهاد وقال الراغب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Qurʾān, given to Muhammad and linked to the surah's opening, guides all people rather than one community, unlike Moses' Book.
rows.anchor: وهذا متعلق بصدر السورة كما مرت الإشارة إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The path called most upright is Islam and monotheism; al-latī omits a noun such as path, state, or community, and al-Alusi finds the deletion more eloquent.
rows.anchor: أقوم الطرق وأسدها أعني ملة الإسلام والتوحيد

rows.speaker: أبو حيان، الرازي
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan and al-Razi say aqwam means upright, not comparative, since other paths lack a shared basis; they compare 98:3 and 98:5.
rows.anchor: الذي يظهر من حيث المعنى أنه لا يراد به التفضيل

rows.speaker: عبد الله، طلحة، ابن وثاب، الإخوان
rows.claim: These readers recite yubashshiru with a lightened form of bashshara.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وطلحة وابن وثاب والإخوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān announces reward for believers who do its righteous acts; the great reward is multiplied tenfold and beyond, and Ibn Jurayj identifies it with Paradise throughout the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: الصالحات ( التي شرحت فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers deny the afterlife and Qurʾānic teachings about resurrection, judgment, and spiritual and bodily recompense; the afterlife is singled out as central and tied to deeds and reward.
rows.anchor: وأحكامها المشروحة فيه من البعث والحساب والجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿtadnā means prepared; the painful punishment is Hell, prepared in the very afterlife they deny, making its unexpected arrival especially dreadful.
rows.anchor: أي أعددنا وهيأنا لهم فيما كفروا به وأنكروا وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People of the Book may be included because they deny bodily recompense and hold baseless afterlife beliefs rather than truly believing the Qurʾānic account.
rows.anchor: ولعل أهل الكتاب داخلون في هذا الحكم لأنهم لا يقولون بالجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment may coordinate with believers' reward as welcome news of the enemy's fate; bashāra may mean any announcement, or an informing verb may be supplied.
rows.anchor: والعطف على أن لهم أجرا كبيرا فيكون إعداد العذاب الأليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives precedence to promise over warning.
rows.anchor: ما في الآية من ترجيح الوعد على الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling believers righteous describes their ideal condition; sinful believers may still enter Paradise through faith and mercy, but highest ranks and honors belong to the righteous.
rows.anchor: فلا بد من التوصيف ولا يلزم منه عدم دخول المفرط الجنة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says only pious believers and unbelievers are mentioned because the intermediate status of grave sinners arose later; Abu Hayyan objects that believers already had lapses in Muhammad's time.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى ذكر المؤمنين الأبرار والكفار ولم يذكر الفسقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilite intermediate position says a major sinner is neither believer nor unbeliever and remains in Hell forever without repentance; most Companions are presumed upright.
rows.anchor: ما ذهب إليه إخوانه المعتزلة من أن مرتكب الكبيرة ليس بمؤمن

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Shaykh al-Islam says the verse depicts the state of the one guided after describing the guide, showing their contrast.
rows.anchor: بيان الحال المهدي إثر بيان حال الهادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-insān may be generic while describing a disbelieving subset, as Ibn Abbas suggests, or describe anyone at moments such as anger, as reports from al-Hasan and Mujahid suggest.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالإنسان الجنس أسند إليه حال بعض أفراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān calls people to the greatest good and warns of greatest evil, but disbelievers ask for punishment, as in 8:32 and 11:32.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن يدعو الإنسان إلى الخير الذي لا خير فوقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request may be a literal prayer or figuratively sinful deeds leading to punishment; some read utterance as sarcastic haste.
rows.anchor: إما بلسانه حقيقة كدأب من قال منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duʿāʾahu means his supplication: omitted mithla and comparison particle make it an accusative verbal noun, like his hypothetical prayer for good.
rows.anchor: أي دعائه فحذف الموصوف وحرف التشبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human in kāna al-insānu ʿajūlan is the same disbelieving person, rashly seeking whatever occurs while blind to harm; the irony is that punishment will come.
rows.anchor: من أسند إليه الدعاء المذكور من أفراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If supplication means sinful actions, haste describes persistent deeds making punishment deserved.
rows.anchor: وعلى تقدير حمل الدعاء على أعمالهم تجعل العجولية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, anyone under anger abandons prayer for good and invokes harm on self, family, or wealth; humans are innately hasty and irritable.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن يدعو الإنسان إلى ما هو خير وهو في بعض أحيانه

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi relates from Aisha that a captive escaped while she was distracted; the Prophet angrily said God cut her hand, then explained he was human and prayed any curse on a believer become purification.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة رضي الله تعالى عنها أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم دخل عليها بأسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans are hasty because they do not deliberate enough to recognize what merits prayer and what deserves protection from.
rows.anchor: وكان الإنسان عجولا غير مستبصر لا يتدبر في أموره حق التدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi accepts the first human as the disbeliever: obedience brings favor, disobedience affliction; after praising Qurʾānic guidance, the passage condemns Quraysh for seeking stones or punishment.
rows.anchor: إرادة الكافر من الإنسان الأول بعض المحققين

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf connects the verse to Qurʾānic guidance: people refuse its best path and choose the most blameworthy one.
rows.anchor: أن القرآن يهديهم للتي هي أقوم ويأبون إلا التي هي ألوم

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: A report from Salman says Adam's head was created first; watching himself form, he urged God to hurry before night while his legs remained unfinished.
rows.anchor: عن سلمان الفارسي قال : أول ما خلق الله تعالى من آدم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also transmits a similar story explaining human haste through Adam.
rows.anchor: وروي نحوه عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi, whose attribution al-Alusi treats cautiously, says Adam saw Paradise's fruit when his spirit reached his eyes and rushed toward it once it entered his stomach.
rows.anchor: لما وصلت الروح لعينيه نظر إلى ثمار الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam's reading makes haste an inherited trait, but al-Alusi prefers generic humanity; the wording can accommodate Adam despite Abu Hayyan's objection.
rows.anchor: والأولى إرادة الجنس وإن كان ألفاظ الآية لا تنبو عن إرادة آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi in both places is most naturally governed by supplication; readings as in or because of are against the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: الباء في الموضعين على ظاهرها صلة الدعاء

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: A report from Jabir says not to pray against oneself, children, or property lest the prayer coincide with an hour when God answers it.
rows.anchor: أبو داود والبزار عن جابر قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This report rebuts the claim that such prayers are never answered out of divine generosity.
rows.anchor: وبه يرد على ما قيل من أن الدعاء بذلك لا يستجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's curse-like words to Aisha are explained as correction in anger, with a request that any undeserved invocation become mercy and purification.
rows.anchor: وأجيب عن ذلك بأنه كان للزجر وإن كان وقت الغضب

rows.speaker: النبي ﷺ
rows.claim: A sound report says the Prophet stipulated that any invocation against a Muslim unworthy of it become purification and nearness to God.
rows.anchor: قال : إني اشترطت على ربي فقلت إنما أنا بشر

rows.speaker: المازري
rows.claim: Al-Maziri, quoted by al-Nawawi, says the Prophet chose between invocation and another correction; anger for God prompted one lawful option, while unworthiness is judged by God's hidden knowledge.
rows.anchor: ما قال المازري من أنه يحتمل أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats phrases such as taribat yamīnuk as habitual Arab speech, not intended curses; fearing accidental acceptance, the Prophet asked to turn them into purification, though al-Alusi cautions that reports have problems.
rows.anchor: ليس بمقصود بل هو مما جرت به عادة العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Standard grammar would retain the wāw in yadʿu without a jussive, but Qurʾānic form is transmitted as heard and not altered to fit a transmitter's judgment.
rows.anchor: إذ لا جازم تحذف له لكن نقل القرآن العظيم كما سمع
